title: A Guide to Indian Saree Fabrics and Weaves, and Where They Come From

body.text: Most Indian saree names are place names. [Kanjeevaram](/collection/fabric/kanjeevaram) comes from Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu, Banarasi from Varanasi, Chanderi and Maheshwari from towns in Madhya Pradesh, Paithani from Paithan in Maharashtra. Once you know that, a great deal of the vocabulary stops being intimidating and starts being geography.
This is a guide to the weaves and fabrics you are most likely to meet, what distinguishes each one, and how to tell what you are holding.
What is the difference between a saree fabric and a weave?
Two different kinds of word get used interchangeably, which is where most of the confusion begins.

**A fabric** describes what the cloth is made of and how it is constructed. [Silk](/collection/fabric/silk), cotton, [chiffon](/collection/fabric/chiffon), [georgette](/collection/fabric/georgette), organza. These say nothing about where the saree was made.

**A weave** describes a tradition tied to a place, with its own techniques, motifs and rules. [Kanjeevaram](/collection/fabric/kanjeevaram), Banarasi, Paithani, Jamdani. These say a great deal about where it was made and how.
So a [Kanjeevaram](/collection/fabric/kanjeevaram) is silk, but not every silk saree is a Kanjeevaram. The fabric is the material. The weave is the lineage.

body.text: What are the main types of silk sarees in India?
Kanjeevaram, Tamil Nadu

Woven in and around Kanchipuram from mulberry silk, and among the heaviest sarees made in India. The distinguishing feature is structural. The body, the border and the pallu are woven separately and then joined, a technique called korvai, which is why the border colour can contrast so completely with the body. Run your finger along the join and you can often feel it.
Look for temple borders, checks, stripes and traditional motifs, with real zari in older pieces.
Banarasi, Uttar Pradesh
Woven in Varanasi, with motifs that carry clear Mughal influence. Floral and foliate patterns, paisleys, and a decorative border edging known as the jhallar.

Banarasi is a family of weaves, not a single thing. Kadhwa is woven motif by motif and can be cut away cleanly on the reverse. Tanchoi is densely patterned with no long floats behind. Jangla covers the whole body in trailing vines. The finer the work, the longer the loom time, sometimes months for one saree.
Mysore silk, Karnataka

Pure mulberry silk, usually with a plain body and a gold zari border, made in Karnataka. The appeal is restraint. Where a Banarasi is dense with pattern, a Mysore silk is smooth, glossy and quiet, and it drapes beautifully because there is so little weight in the body.
Tussar, eastern India

Wild silk, produced in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Bihar and West Bengal, also called kosa. It has a natural honey or beige colour and a slightly uneven texture, without the smooth glow of mulberry silk.
Lighter and more breathable than [Kanjeevaram](/collection/fabric/kanjeevaram), which makes it a warm weather silk. Bhagalpur in Bihar is closely associated with it.
Paithani, Maharashtra
Woven at Paithan and Yeola, using a tapestry technique that produces no wrong side. The pattern reads identically from both faces, which is unusual and is the quickest way to identify one.
The signature motifs are the peacock and the lotus, and the pallu is typically worked in a way that makes it the most valuable part of the saree.
Baluchari, West Bengal
From Bishnupur. The distinguishing feature is narrative. The pallu carries figurative scenes, often drawn from mythology, woven into the cloth, not embroidered on top.
If you are looking at a saree whose pallu tells a story in small figures, this is almost certainly what it is.
Patola, Gujarat

Made in Patan using double ikat, where both the warp and the weft threads are individually tied and dyed before weaving so that the pattern appears when they meet on the loom. Getting the two to align requires extraordinary precision, and a single saree can take many months.
Genuine Patan patola is rare and priced accordingly. Rajkot produces single ikat versions, which are lovely and considerably more available.
Muga, Assam

A wild silk found only in Assam, naturally golden, and unusual in that it is said to gain lustre with washing instead of losing it. Assam also produces pat silk, which is white or cream, and eri, which is softer and warmer.
Which sarees combine silk and cotton?
Chanderi, Madhya Pradesh
Known for a glassy transparency that comes from the way the yarn is prepared. Light, fine, and often woven with small gold motifs scattered across the body.
Comes in silk, cotton, and a silk cotton blend. All three share the same characteristic translucence.
Maheshwari, Madhya Pradesh

From Maheshwar on the Narmada. Lighter than Chanderi, with a reversible border, so the saree can be worn either way round. Stripes and checks are typical, in a cotton silk mix that suits everyday wear.
Gadwal, Telangana

A cotton or cotton silk body attached to a silk border and pallu. The result is a saree that has the presence of silk where it shows and the comfort of cotton where it sits against you. Traditionally light enough to fold into a very small parcel.
Ilkal, Karnataka

From Bagalkot district. A cotton body joined to a silk pallu using a technique called tope teni, where the two are interlocked by hand thread by thread. The pallu is usually red with white patterning.
Which handloom cotton sarees should you know?
Jamdani, West Bengal

Not a fabric but a technique. The pattern is added by hand during weaving, thread by thread, using a supplementary weft, so the motifs seem to float on a sheer ground with no long threads trailing behind. Slow, and among the finest handwork in the subcontinent.
Kota Doria, Rajasthan
From near Kota. Recognisable by its square check structure, created by alternating cotton and silk threads. Very light, almost weightless, and made for heat.
Mangalagiri, Andhra Pradesh
Firm handloom cotton with a zari border and a plain body, the body traditionally left without motifs. Practical, hardwearing and easy to wear often.
What are chiffon, georgette and organza?
These are fabric types, not regional traditions, which is why they are grouped separately.
Chiffon

A sheer plain weave with a soft matte finish, and very light. Originally silk, though much of what is sold now is synthetic. It was adopted by Indian royalty in the early twentieth century and has stayed in the wardrobe ever since, because nothing else drapes quite so fluidly.
Silk chiffon feels warmer to the touch and has a subtler sheen than the synthetic version.
Georgette
Heavier than chiffon, with a faintly crinkled surface and more body. It holds a pleat better and is more forgiving to drape, which is why it suits long occasions.
Organza
Sheer like chiffon but crisp where chiffon is fluid, so it holds its shape and stands slightly away from the body. Silk organza softens with wear. Synthetic organza does not.
How can you tell which weave a saree is?
Start with three questions.

**How heavy is it?** Weight narrows things quickly. A saree you can feel in your forearms is likely a [Kanjeevaram](/collection/fabric/kanjeevaram) or a heavy Banarasi. One you could fold into a handbag is likely Chanderi, Kota or a light cotton.
**Is there a join?** Feel along the border and the pallu. A physical join between differently coloured sections points to [Kanjeevaram](/collection/fabric/kanjeevaram), Gadwal or Ilkal.
**What does the reverse look like?** A pattern that reads perfectly on both faces suggests Paithani. Motifs that appear to float on a sheer ground suggest Jamdani. A blank reverse suggests a machine.

If those three do not settle it, look at the motifs. Peacocks and lotuses point to Paithani. Figurative scenes on the pallu point to Baluchari. Trailing vines and Mughal florals point to Banarasi. Temple borders point south.
To check whether the silk itself is pure, see our guide on [how to identify a pure silk saree](/journal/how-to-identify-pure-silk-saree).
Why does this matter more with preloved sarees?

Many of these weaves are made in far smaller quantities than they once were, and some colour and border combinations are no longer produced at all. A saree from the 1970s in a shade nobody weaves now cannot be reordered.

That is the quiet argument for buying preloved over new. It is not only about cost. Some of the best examples of these traditions already exist, sitting in cupboards, and the only way to own one is to find it.
